titleStmt.title: Chapter 8 — The Shaping of Western Culture — Kullaba - E-Anna instances IV

div.p: In this last chapter of the sequence discussing the instances of historical Kullaba-E-Anna configurations, we concentrate on the medieval and early modern developments which directly contributed to the shaping of Western Culture and therefore to the context discussed in Chapter 2 and the Cornell 7 case itself. Especially meaningful is the notion of stealth religion presented in section 8.2 below. As in the previous three chapters, the numbers in square brackets in section headings refer back to the table in Chapter 4.

div.head: 8.1 [18] The Medieval Compromise — The Three Orders and the Archaic Regression of the West
8.1.1 The Forgotten IE Roots of the Roman West
div.p: The emergence of a renewed trifunctional ideology in Western Europe during the Middle Ages was far from a given historical inevitability. For centuries, the Roman Empire had functioned much more like the highly centralized, bureaucratic Middle Eastern empires of Hammurabi and Ashurbanipal (see Sections 5.3 and 6.1) than like the archaic, trifunctional Kuru-Panchala kingdom of Vedic India (see Section 7.4). The Indo-European roots of Rome were deeply buried in religious remnants that had been almost universally forgotten—such as the three major flamines and the mythological accounts of the early kings of Rome.Georges Dumézil, Archaic Roman Religion, trans. Philip Krapp (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1996), pp. 148-151. Dumézil meticulously excavated these fossilized Indo-European remnants from the bedrock of Roman antiquarianism. He demonstrated that the archaic triad of Jupiter, Mars, and Quirinus, served by the three flamines maiores, perfectly preserved the original trifunctional ideology before it was functionally buried by later Roman syncretism and legalism.

For centuries after the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the intellectual elite of the West (primarily the bishops and abbots) continued to think along the strict clergy/laity dichotomy they shared with the Roman rump state in the East. The Byzantine Empire's E-Anna/Kullaba synthesis, operating in the covert sphere under Justinian (see Section 7.5), owed absolutely nothing to Indo-European trifunctional precedents. It was fundamentally a continuation of the Mesopotamian dual sovereignty model applied to a highly developed, bureaucratic Mediterranean state.

div.head: 8.1.2 The Bankruptcy of the Centralized Imperial Model
div.p: In the West, however, the material and demographic realities no longer supported such a massive administrative apparatus. Despite this, Western European clerics continued for four centuries to attempt to recreate a central authority on the classical Imperial model, aggressively patronizing the Frankish state under the MerovingiansFor the symbiotic relationship between the early medieval Church and the Merovingian dynasty, wherein bishops and monks actively legitimized Frankish martial supremacy in exchange for state protection and patronage, see J. M. Wallace-Hadrill, The Frankish Church (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1983), pp. 55-74. and subsequently the Carolingians.The Carolingian alliance culminated in the papal coronation of Charlemagne in 800 CE, representing a concerted ideological effort by the Latin Church to resurrect a unified, centralized Christian Roman Empire. See Rosamond McKitterick, The Frankish Kingdoms under the Carolingians, 751-987 (London: Longman, 1983), pp. 106-124. They sought a singular, powerful monarch who could act as the secular arm of the Church's Kullaba.

By the middle of the 9th century, the thermodynamic bankruptcy of that strategy was painfully apparent.On the rapid disintegration of the Carolingian imperial project, culminating in the Treaty of Verdun (843) and the subsequent inability of the central monarchy to maintain structural cohesion or defend ecclesiastical institutions from external raids and internal aristocratic predation, see Heinrich Fichtenau, The Carolingian Empire: The Age of Charlemagne, trans. Peter Munz (Oxford: Basil Blackwell, 1957), pp. 177-188. The Carolingian Empire had dissolved into brutal civil war. Worst of all, the central royal authority was proving structurally unable to protect the Church—not to mention the agrarian populace—against the highly decentralized, highly mobile, and constantly shifting menace of the Vikings.Marc Bloch, Feudal Society, trans. L. A. Manyon (London: Routledge, 1961), pp. 15-38. Bloch details how the devastating psychological and institutional impact of the Viking raids exposed the utter inability of the Carolingian central authority to defend its territories, accelerating the fragmentation of power into localized hands. The centralized state had failed, and the local populations were left entirely at the mercy of localized, heavily armed strongmen.

div.head: 8.1.3 The Monks of Auxerre and the Irish Transmission
div.p: This profound existential and institutional crisis prompted two Frankish monks from Auxerre—Haimo and his pupil Heiric—to conceptually reinvent the archaic Indo-European trifunctional structure. They articulated society not as a binary of clergy and laity, but as a functionally interdependent triplet: the oratores (those who pray), the bellatores (those who fight), and the laboratores (those who work).Georges Duby, The Three Orders: Feudal Society Imagined, trans. Arthur Goldhammer (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1980), pp. 99-109. Duby definitively traces the earliest explicit medieval formulations of this trifunctional schema to the intellectual milieu of the Abbey of Saint-Germain d'Auxerre in the 9th century, well before its famous articulation by Adalbero of Laon and Gerard of Cambrai in the 11th century, who had long been thought of as the initiators of the three orders ideology.

As previously established, the Romans had lost all conscious awareness of Indo-European trifunctionality. The Frankish monks possessed only very diluted, textual echoes of it: primarily through a Latin translation of Plato's Timaeus by the late antique philosopher Calcidius, and the Plinian social triplet of senatores, equites, and plebs transmitted through the encyclopedic works of Isidore of Seville. However, this sparse textual transmission has led historians to posit a much more direct, cultural return of trifunctional thinking to the continent via Irish monastic networks.Ireland, having never been conquered or administratively homogenized by the Roman Empire, retained its pristine, archaic Indo-European tripartite social structure (druid/filid, flaith, bóaire). See Alwyn Rees and Brinley Rees, Celtic Heritage: Ancient Tradition in Ireland and Wales (London: Thames and Hudson, 1961), pp. 112-118. Irish monastic foundations across the continent acted as vectors for this un-Romanized intellectual memory. Irish monks had been highly active in the region of Auxerre since the 6th century, and they exerted a profound intellectual influence specifically at the Abbey of Saint-Germain d'Auxerre to which Haimo and Heiric belonged.Pierre Riché, Education and Culture in the Barbarian West, Sixth Through Eighth Centuries, trans. John J. Contreni (Columbia: University of South Carolina Press, 1976), pp. 324-336. Riché details the extensive intellectual networks and cultural influence of Irish and insular monks on the Carolingian continent, establishing them as key vectors for archaic, non-Romanized conceptual frameworks.

Interestingly, this shows that the Irish influenceFor a comprehensive account of the enduring intellectual and theological impact of the Irish diaspora (peregrini) across continental Europe, evolving from the rigorous monastic asceticism of Columbanus in the Merovingian era to the sophisticated philosophical contributions of figures like John Scottus Eriugena in the Carolingian court, see Dáibhí Ó Cróinín, Early Medieval Ireland, 400-1200 (London: Longman, 1995), pp. 195-232. on the continent had shifted from chastising the Merovingian court as a lupanarium (as St. Columbanus did in the 6th century) to advising a return to a much more modest, functional equilibrium by the mid-9th century. During the earlier period, Irish missionaries operated as radical outsiders, launching blistering moral critiques against the overtly Ishtarian excesses of the ascendant Frankish warlords in an attempt to achieve a total moral purification of the BDMB archetype. However, three centuries later, the geopolitical landscape had catastrophically deteriorated. The grand strategy of resurrecting a centralized, Christianized Roman Empire—the Carolingian project—had ended in bankruptcy, dissolving into bitter civil wars and dynastic fracturing. Concurrently, the social positioning of the Irish intellectual diaspora had fundamentally changed; they were no longer wandering ascetics crying in the wilderness, but established masters operating within the prestigious monastic scriptoria of the Carolingian heartland. As the central state evaporated under the relentless pressure of Viking raids and internal collapse, these monks recognized that moral perfectionism was a luxury they could no longer afford. Survival required a pragmatic, localized containment strategy. The trifunctional model was thus deployed not to purify the state, but to functionally harness and limit the violence of the localized bellatores, ensuring the immediate physical survival of the Church and the peasantry.

div.head: 8.1.4 Archaic Regression and the Coalitions of the Meek
div.p: In adopting this trifunctional model, Western Europe effectively bypassed the Augustan, Diocletianic, and Constantinian syntheses, returning to a much more primitive, decentralized version of the dual sovereignty engine. In many ways, it was a profound historical regression—a return to the sociological landscape of the BMAC kavis introducing Varuna (see Section 5.4) to sedate early Indo-Aryan warbands, or even further back to the ancient poet-seers who had originally invented Proto-Indo-European trifunctionality in the 4th millennium BCE somewhere north of Maykop.

This ideological regression, however, provided a brilliantly effective survival mechanism. By explicitly defining the bellatores as a distinct, specialized caste with specific cosmic duties (protecting the Church and the poor), the Kullaba localized its containment strategy. This schema enabled the Western Church to mobilize local coalitions of the meek on the exact model of the old PIE village elders. When the localized E-Anna warlords (the castellans and rogue knights) overstepped their boundaries, the clergy federated the laboratores (the peasantry) to collectively demand thermodynamic regulation. This was spectacularly actualized in the Peace of God and Truce of God movements of the High Middle Ages, where bishops literally marshaled massive crowds of commoners and holy relics to force warlords to swear oaths of non-violence.For the Church's mobilization of the masses against the unchecked mimetic violence of the feudal warlords, see Thomas N. Bisson, The 'Feudal Revolution', Past & Present 142 (1994): 6-42.

This return to a very archaic, but tried and true, trifunctional model of managing the BDMB archetype would play a huge role in shaping the specific, highly localized, and ultimately dynamic aspects of Western Christian culture, differentiating it permanently from the centralized, autocratic trajectories of Byzantium, the Islamic Caliphates, and the successive Kievan and Muscovite Russian states.

div.head: 8.2 [19-20] The Troubadours — Sargonitis, Courtly Love, and the Invention of Stealth Religion
8.2.1 William IX and the Outbreak of Sargonitis
div.p: By the late 11th century, the Catholic Church (the Western Kullaba) had initiated the Gregorian Reform, an aggressive attempt to impose strict paternal-legalist order, eradicate clerical marriage, and firmly subjugate the violence of the feudal bellatores to ecclesiastical authority. It was in this environment of tightening religious regulation that a spectacular, overt flare-up of the ancient E-Anna engine occurred in southern France. Its most famous catalyst was William IX, Duke of Aquitaine (1071–1126), the first historically attested troubadour.For the historical context of William IX and the emergence of troubadour lyric in the politically fragmented environment of the Midi, alongside the encroaching pressures of ecclesiastical reform, see Linda M. Paterson, The World of the Troubadours: Medieval Occitan Society, c. 1100-c. 1300 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993), pp. 1-15.

William IX represents a virulent, localized outbreak of what we might term Sargonitis—the irrepressible urge of the BDMB warlord to explicitly and publicly ground his sovereignty in raw martial-erotic conquest, defiantly bypassing the Kullaba. William’s poetry is shockingly carnal, openly boasting of his sexual exploits and mocking the Church's moral constraints.See Linda M. Paterson, The World of the Troubadours, pp. 28-32. Paterson discusses William IX's scandalous behavior, his excommunications, and his poetry, which oscillates between refined proto-courtliness and boastful obscenity. He famously painted an image of his mistress on his shield so he could bear her in battle, a perfect, literal reincarnation of the Ishtarian hieros gamos paradigm. For William, the Lady was not a chaste spiritual ideal; she was conquered territory, a visceral manifestation of overt porneia granting him the charismatic swagger needed to lead his warband. This was the E-Anna operating in the red once again, for a brief moment.

div.head: 8.2.2 The Eleanor Synthesis: Taming the E-Anna
div.p: However, as history has repeatedly demonstrated (from Naram-Sin to Mark Antony), an overt, unalloyed red state is thermodynamically unsustainable, especially when surrounded by a massive, hostile Kullaba apparatus like the medieval Papacy. The raw Sargonitis of William IX required immediate structural containment. This synthesis was catalyzed in the subsequent generation by his granddaughter, Eleanor of Aquitaine, and her daughter, Marie de Champagne.For the pivotal role of Eleanor and Marie in institutionalizing and refining the courtly love ethos across Northern European courts, transitioning it from raw Occitan lyric into the sophisticated romances of Chrétien de Troyes, see C. Stephen Jaeger, The Origins of Courtliness: Civilizing Trends and the Formation of Courtly Ideals, 939-1210 (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1985), pp. 211-235.

Under their patronage, the raw, carnal lust of the early troubadours was systematically refined and sublimated into fin'amor.The Occitan term fin'amor translates literally as refined love or pure love, distinguishing it conceptually from fals'amor (false, purely carnal love), and signaling the deliberate ideological sublimation of raw eros into a spiritually and socially elevating aristocratic ethos. The sexually available woman of William's poetry was elevated into the midonsThe term midons is a grammatical anomaly in Old Occitan. Derived from the Latin meus dominus (my lord), it is a masculine noun applied to a female object of devotion, explicitly mapping the hierarchical, political subjugation of the feudal vassal onto the erotic submission of the lover. (my lord)—a Platonic, inaccessible ideal. This ideological operation masterfully blended the E-Anna's charismatic allure with the Kullaba's demand for chastity, heavily utilizing Marian overtones to sanitize the idolatry.For the complex interplay and mutual borrowing between the secular veneration of the midons and the escalating monastic theology surrounding the Virgin Mary, particularly championed by figures like Bernard of Clairvaux, see Jaroslav Pelikan, Mary Through the Centuries: Her Place in the History of Culture (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1996), pp. 137-152. The violent, rape-prone energy of the knight was redirected into a posture of perpetual, unconsummated, subservient devotion to the Lady. The E-Anna engine was still running—generating immense mimetic devotion and martial prestige for the aristocratic caste—but the fist had been safely placed back inside a velvet, Christian-looking glove.

div.head: 8.2.3 Catharism, Rougemont, and the Birth of Stealth Religion
div.p: This sublimation of the E-Anna reached its most complex psychological phase in the late 12th and early 13th centuries, against the backdrop of the Cathar heresy in Languedoc. In his seminal work Love in the Western World, Denis de Rougemont identified profound structural affinities between the refined poetry of the troubadours and the dualistic, flesh-rejecting theology of the Cathars.Denis de Rougemont, Love in the Western World, trans. Montgomery Belgion (New York: Pantheon Books, 1956), pp. 77-110. Rougemont famously argued that the Lady of the troubadours was a coded representation of the Cathar Church of Love, and that courtly love was a fundamentally heretical death-drive. While historians have hotly debated whether the troubadours were literal crypto-heretics, the dual sovereignty framework renders a literal conspiracy theory unnecessary. What emerged under the patronage of figures like Garsenda of Forcalquier—especially after the Albigensian Crusade brutally crushed overt religious heterodoxy—was something much more sophisticated: the invention of stealth religion.

Stealth religion is a psychological, semi-conscious trick. It allows the individual to safely claim the civic and social identity of a good, orthodox Christian (submitting to the Kullaba) while simultaneously indulging in the transgressive, mimetic theology of the E-Anna. The knight or poet worships an inaccessible idol-lady with the exact same ecstatic, all-consuming devotion previously reserved for Ishtar (or the Cathar Church of Love), but because the idol is conceptually severed from official state theology, the Inquisition cannot easily prosecute it. The aristocracy absorbed the rebellious, elitist spirit of the Cathar episode, but deployed it as an internalized, psychological aesthetic rather than a rival Church.

div.head: 8.2.4 The Secular Entertainment Loophole — Virtualizing the E-Anna
div.p: The key to successfully operating this stealth religion is the framing device. The medieval aristocracy achieved this massive cognitive dissonance by cordoning off their E-Anna worship under the newly minted category of secular entertainment and lyrical poetry. By insisting that the passionate, idolizing, and often adulterous devotion to the Lady was merely a game of the courts, a literary fiction, or a performance of innocent-looking fin'amor, the bellatores created a massive juridical loophole.

The Catholic Kullaba, which excelled at identifying and crushing overt rival cults (like the Cathars), was poorly equipped to prosecute fiction. This brilliant liminal adaptation allowed the martial caste to retain their autonomous, charismatic E-Anna ideology—the very engine that made them feel like demigods—while remaining integrated within the Catholic political structure. This concept of secular entertainment as a Trojan horse for covert E-Anna idolatry is a momentous historical innovation. It is a psychological technology promised to a spectacularly bright future in Western culture, eventually mutating into the modern cults of celebrity, romantic cinema, and pop-culture fandom, where the masses safely worship BDMBs and Ishtarian avatars under the unassailable alibi of just consuming media.

With the three Orders (Section 8.1) and the stealth religion of fin'amor, Medieval Western Christianity comes very close to emulating Sassanid Persia (Section 7.2). By this point, Western Christianity has come as close as it could to an overt E-Anna, while it is also developing quasi-gnostic theology (Duns ScotusThe Franciscan theologian John Duns Scotus radically departed from the Thomistic tradition of the analogia entis (analogy of being) by asserting the univocity of being (univocatio entis)—the proposition that the concept of being possesses the exact same fundamental meaning whether applied to God or to created entities. Scholars associated with the Radical Orthodoxy movement, such as John Milbank, have argued that this conceptual flattening inadvertently resuscitated a form of intellectual gnosis within Christian theology. By encapsulating God and creation within a single overarching metaphysical category, Scotus circumvented the transcendent apophatic mystery of the divine, implying that human rational faculties could directly and conceptually grasp God's essence. This reduction dismantled the participatory ontology of the earlier medieval synthesis, paving the way for nominalism, modern secularism, and an essentially gnostic confidence in human reason's capacity to master reality. See John Milbank, Theology and Social Theory: Beyond Secular Reason (Oxford: Blackwell, 1990), pp. 302-306.) and the ever more pharisaic Canon Law. It is clearly ripe for reform.

It is noteworthy that the resemblance between the Sassanian period in Iran and medieval Europe is not only religious. Sassanian Iran also had its military gentry class of heavy cavalrymen who formed the backbone of the Royal army and lived in fortified manors. These elite mounted warriors, the aswārān, drawn primarily from the dehqān class of landed nobility, structurally mirrored the feudal bellatores. This deep sociological parallel created a nearly identical martial ecosystem, pulling the West towards similar ideological patterns to integrate a powerful, localized warrior elite into the broader religious and political order.For detailed historical scholarship on the Sassanian military gentry, their role as the heavily armored cavalry backbone of the army, and their socioeconomic foundation in rural fortified manors, see Kaveh Farrokh, Sassanian Elite Cavalry AD 224-642 (Oxford: Osprey Publishing, 2005); and Touraj Daryaee, Sasanian Persia: The Rise and Fall of an Empire (London: I.B. Tauris, 2009), pp. 45-51.

div.head: 8.2.5 The House of Garsenda
div.p: The staggering sociopolitical efficacy of this new, sublimated E-Anna engine is empirically verifiable in the dynastic trajectory of its primary operators. A striking illustration of this phenomenon was highlighted by Matt Baker, the host of the UsefulCharts educational platform.See Matt Baker, The Most Powerful Matrilineal Dynasty in History, UsefulCharts (YouTube, 2020), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sl4WtajjMks. Baker traced a massive, highly influential Matrilineal Dynasty directly back to Garsenda of Forcalquier—the aforementioned patroness of the troubadours (and a trobairitz herself) who was deeply embedded in the stealth religion culture of the South of France.

Reinforcing this genealogical finding is the remarkable fate of Garsenda's four granddaughters (the daughters of her son, Ramon Berenguer V of Provence). Despite not possessing overwhelmingly vast territorial dowries, all four sisters married into the highest echelons of European royalty: Margaret married Louis IX of France; Eleanor married Henry III of England; Sanchia married Richard of Cornwall (King of Germany, who contested the Holy Roman Empire with Alfonso X of Castile); and Beatrice married Charles I of Anjou (King of Sicily).For a detailed historical account of the spectacular marital alliances of the four daughters of Ramon Berenguer V and Beatrice of Savoy (Garsenda's daughter-in-law), and the subsequent political influence they wielded across thirteenth-century Europe, see Margaret Howell, Eleanor of Provence: Queenship in Thirteenth-Century England (Oxford: Blackwell, 1998), pp. 1-13. Within the dual sovereignty framework, this spectacular dynastic success is not a mere coincidence; it is the direct consequence of the enormous Ishtarian prestige generated by the literary activity of their grandmother and the cultural phenomenon of fin'amor. Garsenda and her descendants effectively monopolized the stealth E-Anna charismatic capital of the era. The most powerful monarchs in Europe (the ultimate BDMBs) inherently recognized that aligning their dynasties with the House of Garsenda provided access to the premier source of sublimated martial-erotic legitimacy available in the High Middle Ages. This mechanism explains how the secular entertainment loophole and its associated covert-in-plain-sight E-Anna engine spread like wildfire through the European nobility.

div.head: 8.3 [21] Frederick II Hohenstaufen — The Preambulus Antichristi and the E-Anna's Neoplatonic Rebellion
8.3.1 A Macro-Outbreak of Sargonitis: The Stupor Mundi
div.p: Frederick II Hohenstaufen (1194–1250) represents a systemic, macro-level outbreak of Sargonitis, dwarfing the localized, poetic rebellion of William IX of Aquitaine a century earlier. Frederick, known by his contemporaries as the stupor mundi (wonder of the world), deliberately constructed a court in Palermo that operated as the absolute, thermodynamic antithesis of the Catholic Kullaba. He exhibited all the quintessential attributes of an unrestrained BDMB: he maintained a lavish royal harem guarded by eunuchs, paraded exotic menageries across Europe to generate intense mimetic awe among the populace, and famously employed a standing army of Saracens from Lucera. Because these Muslim mercenaries were completely immune to the Papacy's primary weapon of control—excommunication—they provided Frederick with a kinetic, martial fist entirely insulated from the Church's thermodynamic regulation.See David Abulafia, Frederick II: A Medieval Emperor (London: Allen Lane, 1988), pp. 146-148. Abulafia details the strategic brilliance of the Lucera settlement, noting that Frederick's Saracen troops formed the unshakeable, non-Christian core of his military power in Italy, acting entirely outside papal jurisdiction.

The cultural transmission of this E-Anna energy was direct and dynastic. Through his marriage to Constance of Aragon, Frederick became the brother-in-law of Alfonso II of Provence, the husband of the powerful troubadour patroness Garsenda of Forcalquier (see Section 8.2). This vital dynastic link provided a direct conduit for the stealth religion of fin'amor and Occitan lyricism to flow directly into the Sicilian court. The famed Sicilian School of poetry, which birthed the Italian sonnet, was essentially a transplant of the E-Anna's charismatic literary apparatus into the imperial core, weaponized to glorify the emperor and his courtiers.

div.head: 8.3.2 The Anti-Kullaba Weapon: Neoplatonism and the Sicilian Bureaucracy
div.p: Frederick’s true structural genius, however, lay in realizing that a BDMB could not effectively rule a vast empire solely with Saracen swords and love poetry; he needed to permanently break the Papacy's absolute monopoly on the First Function (literacy, law, and administration). Rather than submitting to the Catholic Kullaba for his administrators, Frederick decided to engineer his own, competing E-Anna bureaucracy. To forge its ideological foundation, he merged the Occitan poetic tradition with a resurgent Neoplatonism.

He achieved this through massive state sponsorship of a translation movement. Frederick actively patronized Jewish scholars from the Holy Land, Egypt, and Tunisia, such as Jacob Anatoli,Jacob Anatoli (c. 1194–1256) was a prominent Jewish scholar invited to Frederick's court in Naples and Palermo, where he translated Ptolemy, Averroes, and Maimonides into Latin and Hebrew. See Colette Sirat, A History of Jewish Philosophy in the Middle Ages (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1985), pp. 226-227. alongside Christian translators with deep Arabic connections like Michael Scot.Michael Scot (c. 1175–c. 1232) served as astrologer to Frederick II and systematically translated Aristotle and Averroes from Arabic. See Charles Homer Haskins, Studies in the History of Mediaeval Science (Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1924), pp. 272-298. These scholars translated philosophical, scientific, and astrological texts from Arabic and Hebrew into Latin.The most structurally critical of these translated texts included Aristotle's Historia Animalium, De Caelo, and De Anima with Averroes's commentaries, Ptolemy's Almagest, and the philosophical writings of Maimonides. Frederick's own masterpiece on falconry, De arte venandi cum avibus, relies heavily on the Aristotelian scientific corpus translated by Scot. See David Abulafia, Frederick II: A Medieval Emperor (London: Allen Lane, 1988), pp. 254-260. By establishing the University of Naples in 1224—history's first state university created entirely independent of the Church—Frederick built a secular factory for administrators whose loyalty was bound exclusively to the Emperor. He effectively staffed his state apparatus with his own E-Anna men, completely bypassing the traditional Western literati's institutional loyalty to Rome. In so doing, Frederick II continued the absorption process of Arabic philosophical culture that had started to trickle into Europe since the previous century through Sicily and Muslim Spain into Italy and the Rhineland on the one hand, and into Occitan-speaking Southwestern France (where Catharism had flourished) on the other.For the transmission of this Arabic philosophical and scientific culture, and its role in challenging orthodox Western epistemology, see María Rosa Menocal, The Arabic Role in Medieval Literary History: A Forgotten Heritage (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1987), pp. 27-35. Menocal highlights how the troubadours and Cathar networks actively metabolized these Eastern esoteric and dualist undercurrents.

div.head: 8.3.3 Bolstering Rougemont: The Elitist Spirit of Gnostic Dualism and Neoplatonism
div.p: The philosophical climate of Frederick's court provides a striking corroboration of Denis de Rougemont's thesis linking the troubadours to Catharism. While classical Neoplatonism and Dualistic Gnosticism (Catharism) possess obvious technical theological differences, structurally and sociologically they share a profound homology: they exude a knowledge-based, elitist, and mystical atmosphere that completely bypasses the orthodox, incarnational, and egalitarian theology of the Christian Kullaba.

Frederick’s inner circle of philosophers and poets did not revere him as a pious, submissive son of the Church; they effectively worshipped him as a quasi-divine, messianic intellect—an earthly embodiment of the Active Intellect itself.See Ernst Kantorowicz, Frederick the Second, 1194-1250, trans. E. O. Lorimer (New York: Frederick Ungar, 1957), pp. 251-256. Kantorowicz masterfully captures how Frederick's court generated an aura of divine, intellectual absolutism around the Emperor, treating him as a terrestrial savior of justice and reason independent of Papal mediation. This represents an incredibly sophisticated evolution of the E-Anna engine: substituting the physical martial-erotic goddess with the intoxicating, mimetic allure of forbidden, esoteric knowledge (the feminine Sofia, the intellectualized avatar of Ishtar), allowing the sovereign to be directly deified by his own administrators without requiring the Kullaba's permission. Jeffrey Epstein, with his dual entourage of Victoria's Secret models and theoretical physicists, is the latest heir of the self-deification tradition started by Frederick II.Just as Frederick II bypassed the orthodox clergy by patronizing esoteric philosophers and astrologers to create a self-deifying inner circle, Epstein utilized his immense wealth to cultivate a private court where two groups mingled: elite scientists (physicists, evolutionary biologists) on the one hand and elite international models of the Victoria's Secret kind on the other. This pursuit of esoteric gnosis (e.g., transhumanism, eugenics) allied with classic erotic E-Anna prestige provided a quasi-divine aura that mimetically compelled an infinite array of top personalities to perform the ritual pilgrimage to Epstein's Island. For a structural analysis of this dynamic, see Evgeny Morozov, The Epstein Ideology, The New Republic (2019), which discusses how Epstein’s cultivation of elite scientific networks functioned as an ideological shield and a modern esoteric religion. This lineage of rogue BDMBs utilizing esoteric intellect to bypass the Kullaba includes Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta,Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta (1417–1468), Lord of Rimini, constructed the Tempio Malatestiano, which explicitly blended Neoplatonic paganism with the deification of his mistress, Isotta degli Atti. Pope Pius II notoriously condemned him to Hell for heresy, incest, and operating a pagan cult. See Anthony F. D'Elia, Pagan Virtue in a Christian World: Sigismondo Malatesta and the Italian Renaissance (Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2006), pp. 1-15. Emperor Rudolf II,Rudolf II (1552–1612), Holy Roman Emperor, largely abandoned Catholic Kullaba administration, retreating to Prague to immerse himself in alchemy, Neoplatonic occultism, and a massive collection of art and concubines. See R. J. W. Evans, Rudolf II and His World: A Study in Intellectual History, 1576-1612 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1973), pp. 196-242. Raimondo di Sangro,Raimondo di Sangro (1710–1771), Prince of Sansevero, was a notorious Neapolitan inventor, alchemist, and freemason whose esoteric Chapel of Sansevero and rumored magical powers provoked intense conflict with the Church. See Harold Acton, The Bourbons of Naples (1734-1825) (London: Methuen, 1956), pp. 84-88. the Count of Cagliostro,Alessandro Cagliostro (1743–1795), occultist and founder of Egyptian Freemasonry, claimed immense esoteric power and engaged in scandalous court affairs, directly challenging orthodox ecclesiastical authority. See Iain McCalman, The Last Alchemist: Count Cagliostro, Master of Magic in the Age of Reason (New York: HarperCollins, 2003), pp. 45-60. the Comte de Saint-Germain,The Comte de Saint-Germain (c. 1712–1784) was a mysterious alchemist and courtier who projected an aura of immortality and esoteric wisdom, mingling with the French royal court while bypassing conventional rational and ecclesiastical authority. See Colin Wilson, The Occult: A History (London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1971), pp. 421-426. the Marquis de Sade,The Marquis de Sade (1740–1814) weaponized extreme, philosophical materialism to justify unrestrained, violent sexual gratification, explicitly mocking the Catholic Kullaba and formulating a dark anti-theology of the BDMB. See Francine du Plessix Gray, At Home with the Marquis de Sade: A Life (New York: Simon and Schuster, 1998), pp. 130-145. and Aleister CrowleyAleister Crowley (1875–1947), founder of the religion of Thelema, utilized explicit sex magic and esoteric gnosis to create a modern, cultic E-Anna, actively defying Victorian and Christian moral norms. See Richard Kaczynski, Perdurabo: The Life of Aleister Crowley (Berkeley: North Atlantic Books, 2010), pp. 200-220., with his legion of pop music and underground imitators, one of whom, Lou Reed, might well have been one of Epstein's teachers in devilryBoth were from the same Jewish New York middle class background and grew up in a similar cultural environment. Reed only practiced his devilry as a pose, while Epstein went further in its implementation. Yet their physical appearance and dark persona are eerily similar..

div.head: 8.3.4 The Augustan Revival and the Preambulus Antichristi
div.p: Frederick supplemented this philosophical rebellion by heavily leveraging pre-Christian, Augustan elements to visually bypass the papal narrative. He minted the augustalis, a magnificent gold coin explicitly depicting himself in the guise of a classical Roman emperor, and erected the monumental Capua Gate. This structure deliberately revived ancient imperial Roman architectural iconography to project an aura of unmediated, terrestrial supremacy directly linked to the pagan past.

The response from the ultimate Kullaba—the Papacy—was total, apocalyptic warfare. This was not a synthesis; it was open, institutional conflict. Pope Gregory IX and his successor Innocent IV excommunicated Frederick multiple times. In a famous encyclical of 1239,This encyclical explicitly drew upon Revelation 13, framing Frederick not as a secular political rival, but as an apocalyptic monstrosity emerging from the abyss to destroy the Church. See David Abulafia, Frederick II, pp. 345-346. Gregory IX explicitly designated the Emperor as the preambulus Antichristi (the forerunner of the Antichrist), deploying apocalyptic imagery against the Emperor:

cit.quote: A beast has risen from the sea, full of words of blasphemy... look carefully at the head, the middle and the lower parts of this beast, Frederick, the so-called Emperor.
cit.bibl: Pope Gregory IX, Encyclical Ascendit de mari bestia (1239), quoted in Ernst Kantorowicz, Frederick the Second, p. 500.

div.p: The Pope rightly recognized that Frederick was not merely a disobedient king requesting political concessions, but an existential threat operating a rival, self-sustaining E-Anna sovereignty engine that threatened to render the Church obsolete.

div.head: 8.3.5 A Retrospective Window into Uruk
div.p: The era of Frederick II gives us a highly documented, retrospective window into what the original friction between the two sacred precincts of Late Chalcolithic Uruk must have looked like. When the Babylonian or Augustan synthesis fails—when the E-Anna refuses to wear the Kullaba glove, and the Kullaba refuses to legitimize the BDMB's fist—the result is total, unmediated institutional warfare.

Just as the Papacy deployed interdicts, excommunications, coalitions of the meek (the Lombard League), and apocalyptic propaganda to destroy the Hohenstaufen E-Anna, we can postulate that the original ensi of the Anu precinct in Uruk deployed the divine terrors of the sky god against rogue lugal who had grown too powerful through the mimetic contagion of Inanna. Frederick's eventual defeat, and the total, ruthless annihilation of his bloodline by the Papacy's proxies after his death, empirically demonstrates why the dual sovereignty synthesis is a thermodynamic necessity: without the stabilizing mechanism of the Kullaba's cosmic endorsement, the BDMB state is eventually isolated, surrounded by hostile coalitions, and crushed.

div.head: 8.4 [22-23] Joan of Arc — The Desperate Epiphany and the Return to the Black
8.4.1 A Desperate Move, Not a Calculated Sargonitis
div.p: By 1429, the Valois monarchy was in a state of terminal, thermodynamic collapse. Charles VII was trapped in the Loire Valley, having lost control of both his capital and the traditional coronation site.Following the devastating defeat at Agincourt (1415) and the Treaty of Troyes (1420), Charles VII was effectively disinherited. Paris and Reims were under Anglo-Burgundian control, leaving the King of Bourges geographically and politically stranded south of the Loire. See Christopher Allmand, The Hundred Years War: England and France at War c.1300-c.1450 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1988), pp. 28-32. More devastatingly, the English and Burgundian alliance had effectively captured the institutional high ground of the Catholic Kullaba in the north, monopolizing the University of Paris and the regional ecclesiastical hierarchy to systematically delegitimize Charles's right to rule.The University of Paris, acting as the supreme theological and intellectual authority in Northern Europe, actively backed the Anglo-Burgundian regime, providing the necessary ecclesiastical and intellectual glove to legitimize the English claim to the French throne. See Colette Beaune, The Birth of an Ideology: Myths and Symbols of Nation in Late-Medieval France, trans. Susan Ross Huston (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1991), pp. 15-25. It was in this environment of absolute existential desperation that the E-Anna engine dramatically, and shockingly, flared back into the red.

It is highly improbable that Charles VII had read Herodotus, or that his courtiers deliberately sought to re-enact Peisistratos's chariot entry into Athens alongside the faux-goddess Phye. Charles was not exhibiting a megalomaniacal outbreak of Sargonitis, as William IX or Frederick II had done; he was a weak, vacillating monarch grasping at straws. Yet, by arraying Joan of Arc—a teenage virgin claiming direct, unmediated divine instruction—in custom-made white armor and placing her at the vanguard of his army, the French court pulled off an almost identical, archaic structural maneuver. They bypassed the hostile, administrative Kullaba entirely by unleashing a direct, terrifying, and awe-inspiring manifestation of the martial-erotic goddess archetype onto the battlefield.For the deliberate visual and ideological staging of Joan by the Armagnac court—including the provision of custom plate armor and a specialized battle standard to maximize her charismatic impact on the troops—see Craig Taylor, Joan of Arc: La Pucelle (Manchester: Manchester University Press, 2006), pp. 55-63.

div.head: 8.4.2 The Astonishing Robustness of the E-Anna Archetype
div.p: What is truly staggering about the Joan of Arc episode is the empirical proof it provides for the sheer sociopsychological robustness of the dual sovereignty engine. Nearly two millennia after Peisistratos, and after a thousand years of rigorous, official Christianization and theological policing by the Church, the deep cultural programming of the masses remained intact. The people—and more importantly, the brutal, demoralized, and illiterate soldiers of the French army—instantly recognized the archetype.

They did not demand theological treatises or Papal bulls; the visual spectacle of the armed virgin riding under a banner was sufficient to trigger an overwhelming mimetic contagion. The crushing lethargy of the French troops vanished overnight, replaced by a fanatical, kinetic energy. The E-Anna engine immediately galvanized the warband, allowing them to break the Siege of Orléans and reverse the entire momentum of the Hundred Years' War.On the instantaneous transformation of French military morale and the subsequent string of unprecedented victories (the Loire campaign) triggered exclusively by Joan's charismatic presence, see Kelly DeVries, Joan of Arc: A Military Leader (Stroud: Sutton Publishing, 1999), pp. 70-90. DeVries emphasizes that her impact was primarily psychological and mimetic, overriding the strategic caution of veteran commanders. The phenomenon effortlessly proved that the primal, BDMB-authorizing technology of the ancient Near East was merely dormant in the European psyche, not extinct.

div.head: 8.4.3 Reims as the New Akitu and Banais Ríghi
div.p: The campaign culminated in the march to Reims for the anointing of the King. Within our framework, this event is not merely a Christian sacrament; it is the structural parallel of the Babylonian Akitu festival or the ancient Celtic banais ríghi (the wedding of kingship to the sovereignty goddess).In archaic Celtic ideology, the legitimate king must ritually mate with the goddess of the land (the sovereignty goddess) to validate his martial and fertility mandate. See Proinsias Mac Cana, Celtic Mythology (London: Hamlyn, 1970), pp. 117-121. The presence of the armed maiden at the anointing structurally fulfills this exact Indo-European requirement. During the coronation, Joan stood prominently beside Charles VII, holding her battle standard. By visually acting as his divine, charismatic sponsor, she performed the exact same function as Ishtar confirming the martial-erotic fitness of the Mesopotamian monarch. Charles VII was transformed from a discredited dauphin into a divinely mandated sovereign, completely circumventing the English-controlled Kullaba apparatus in Paris.For the ideological necessity of the anointing at Reims and Joan's central visual role in confirming Charles's legitimacy against the rival Anglo-Burgundian narrative, see Deborah A. Fraioli, Joan of Arc: The Early Debate (Woodbridge: Boydell Press, 2000), pp. 45-58.

div.head: 8.4.4 Cauchon and the Confused Kullaba
div.p: The reaction of the hostile Anglo-Burgundian establishment, embodied by Bishop Pierre Cauchon,Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais, orchestrated Joan's trial. As a leading cleric tied to the University of Paris and the Anglo-Burgundian alliance, he represents the quintessential hostile Kullaba operative attempting to neutralize a rogue charismatic threat. See Charles Wayland Lightbody, The Judgements of Joan: Joan of Arc, a Study in Cultural History (Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1961), pp. 112-130. perfectly illustrates the institutional limitations of the Christian Kullaba when confronted with a raw, red E-Anna manifestation. The ecclesiastical authorities recognized the terrifying thermodynamic threat Joan posed, but they lacked the correct diagnostic vocabulary. Cauchon and the inquisitors attempted to kill the myth by utilizing their standard legalistic tools—branding her a heretic, a cross-dresser, and a witch.The trial transcripts meticulously document the Inquisition's attempt to force Joan's charismatic behavior (particularly her male military attire and direct divine revelations) into standard categories of heresy and witchcraft, demonstrating the Kullaba's desperate need to categorize and neutralize anomalous E-Anna energy. See W. S. Scott, trans., The Trial of Joan of Arc (London: Folio Society, 1956).

However, this juridical response proved incredibly clumsy and ultimately ineffective at killing the underlying archetype. The trial reveals a Church that was profoundly ill at ease dealing with such primal forces; the theologians had forgotten more about the ancient patterns of sovereignty justification than the illiterate peasantry had. By burning Joan at the stake, Cauchon succeeded in destroying the physical avatar, but he spectacularly failed to extinguish the mimetic contagion. Her martyrdom permanently cemented the E-Anna's charismatic endorsement of the Valois dynasty.Marina Warner, Joan of Arc: The Image of Female Heroism (New York: Knopf, 1981), pp. 160-180. Warner analyzes how the martyrdom instantly transformed Joan from a vulnerable political pawn into an untouchable, eternal mythic symbol.

div.head: 8.4.5 The Nullification Trial: E-Anna and Kullaba Reconciled
div.p: By 1456, the thermodynamic crisis had passed. Charles VII had decisively won the war and expelled the English. Unlike the megalomaniacal Frederick II, Charles was a pragmatic politician who understood that to consolidate his dynasty and govern a stabilized realm, he needed to permanently heal the rift with the universal Kullaba (the Papacy). He could not rule indefinitely on the volatile, chaotic fumes of Joan's martial ecstasy.

The Nullification TrialThe Nullification Trial (1455-1456), authorized by Pope Callixtus III, systematically dismantled the verdict of 1431, effectively clearing Joan of heresy while carefully ensuring her actions were legally subordinated to orthodox Catholic interpretation. See Malcolm G. A. Vale, Charles VII (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1974), pp. 55-60. (the Rehabilitation) was the required structural synthesis. Orchestrated with the cooperation of Rome, the trial retroactively sanitized Joan's transgressive, boundary-breaking energy. The Church officially accepted her intervention as a divine miracle, but strictly circumscribed it as a unique, unrepeatable event of the past. By officially clearing her name, Charles VII safely integrated the charismatic E-Anna capital into his official, legalistic legacy, while simultaneously vowing implicit submission to the Church's ultimate interpretive authority. The goddess was accepted, but firmly placed back into the black. The classical Ishtarian fist in the Kullaba glove was successfully restored in France.This institutional maneuver allowed the French Crown to claim divine martial endorsement without continually threatening the ecclesiastical hierarchy, achieving a perfect, black dual sovereignty synthesis characteristic of the late medieval nation-state.

div.head: 8.4.6 A Ridiculous Post-Scriptum: Canonization and Nationalism
div.p: The ultimate post-scriptum to the Joan of Arc episode occurred centuries later, culminating in her beatification (1909) and canonization (1920) by the Roman Catholic Church. By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the traditional Catholic Kullaba had been stripped of its temporal power and faced the overwhelming, mass-mimetic engine of modern Nationalism. In a desperate, clumsy attempt to adapt to this new sociopolitical reality, the Church formally elevated the ultimate French nationalist icon to the altars.For the political context of Joan's canonization—specifically the Vatican's attempt to reconcile with the deeply secular, anti-clerical Third French Republic by co-opting the premier symbol of French patriotism—see Colette Beaune, Joan of Arc, trans. Gregory Elliott (Cambridge: Polity Press, 2001), pp. 320-335.

This canonization represents a bizarre historical irony. The very institution that had originally burned the avatar of the E-Anna because it could not tolerate her unmediated, martial-charismatic threat, retroactively embraced her in a vain attempt to co-opt the secular religion of the modern nation-state. It is a revealing epilogue that highlights the enduring, combustible power of the archaic BDMB/warrior-goddess archetype, and the perpetual, occasionally desperate efforts of administrative bureaucracies to capture its fire.

div.head: 8.5 [24] Louis XIV and Versailles — The Zenith of the Secular E-Anna
8.5.1 The Trauma of the Fronde and the rise of the Palace
div.p: When the young Louis XIV assumed personal control of the French state, he was deeply scarred by the trauma of the Fronde (1648–1653)—a chaotic, highly destructive civil war initiated by the high nobility and the Parlement of Paris.For a comprehensive history of the Fronde and its devastating psychological impact on the young Louis XIV, cementing his lifelong determination to break the independent political power of the nobility and the judiciary, see A. Lloyd Moote, The Revolt of the Judges: The Parlement of Paris and the Fronde, 1643-1652 (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1971), pp. 350-375. The Fronde empirically demonstrated that the Medieval Compromise had ceased to operate; the bellatores could no longer be contained by the traditional Catholic Kullaba alone. To completely break the independent martial power of the aristocracy, Louis XIV required a solution that did not rely on endless, localized military suppression. Like Charles VII before him, Louis leaned decisively into the E-Anna engine to consolidate his sovereignty, although he executed this maneuver in a far more calculated, enduring, and less chaotic manner.

His solution was Versailles. To understand Versailles, one must recognize the deep history of its architectural form. The dedicated royal palace first emerged in Early Dynastic Sumer as the e-galOn the architectural emergence of the e-gal in Early Dynastic Mesopotamia as a distinct physical and institutional separation of the martial king (lugal) from the temple priesthood (en/ensi), establishing the foundational spatial dichotomy of dual sovereignty, see Michael Roaf, Cultural Atlas of Mesopotamia and the Ancient Near East (New York: Facts on File, 1990), p. 78. (Great House), separating the martial warlord from the temple priesthood. This concept migrated almost immediately to Egypt, where the word PharaohThe Egyptian term pr-ˤ3 (Pharaoh) literally translates to Great House or palace. Originally referring solely to the royal estate, by the New Kingdom, the term had become the primary metonymy for the living god-king himself. See Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2000), p. 227. (literally also Great House) became the ultimate metonymy for the sovereign himself. The very word palace is a direct etymological descendant of the Palatine Hill in Rome, the site of Augustus's imperial residence.See Frank Sear, Roman Architecture (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1983), p. 134. The transition of the Palatine Hill from a residential neighborhood to a singular, monumental manifestation of the Emperor's physical and political body permanently inextricably linked the concept of the palace with BDMB autocratic rule. Palaces have functioned ever since as the essential, physical symbol of BDMB rule—a heavily symbolic E-Anna precinct completely dominated by the person of the monarch.

div.head: 8.5.2 The Maîtresse-en-Titre and the Secular Spectacle
div.p: Louis XIV populated his new E-Anna by institutionalizing and expanding preexisting technologies of charismatic control. Foremost among these was the maîtresse-en-titre (official royal mistress), an institution formally pioneered by Charles VII with Agnès Sorel.Agnès Sorel was the first woman to be officially recognized as the maîtresse-en-titre, explicitly formalizing the E-Anna dynamic at the French court by transforming the King's adultery into a public, quasi-institutionalized office of state. See Tracy Adams, The Life and Afterlife of Isabeau of Bavaria (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2010), pp. 225-228. Louis bound this overt display of sexual, transgressive dominance together with the stealth religion of secular entertainment. By patronizing the theatrical genius of Molière, the musical grandiosity of Jean-Baptiste Lully, and orchestrating relentless court feasting and ballet, Louis constructed a largely virtual, but extraordinarily visible, version of the ancient E-Anna.

In this environment, the king himself literally danced on stage as Apollo, the Sun King. While the iconography was nominally Apollonian (Kullaba), the structural reality was pure Ishtar. The monarch's physical body became the supreme object of aesthetic and erotic veneration, successfully mesmerizing the entire court.For the definitive analysis of Louis XIV's deliberate, political deployment of court spectacle, ballet, and the royal body to domesticate the nobility and centralize charismatic authority, see Jean-Marie Apostolidès, Le Roi-machine: Spectacle et politique au temps de Louis XIV (Paris: Minuit, 1981), pp. 45-68.

div.head: 8.5.3 The Mimetic Magnet of Versailles
div.p: The mimetic gravitational pull of Versailles was staggering. It acted as an irresistible magnet, attracting and permanently fixing the rebellious grands of the Fronde era like iron filings. Louis XIV did not need to besiege their castles; he simply made absence from the E-Anna social suicide. A typical day at Versailles was a masterclass in mimetic spectacle. From the levé (the ceremonial waking of the king) to the coucher, every physical movement of the BDMB was sacralized. Aristocrats who had previously waged war against the crown now engaged in vicious, petty mimetic rivalry over the right to hold the king's candlestick or hand him his shirt.The foundational sociological analysis of this mechanism is Norbert Elias, The Court Society, trans. Edmund Jephcott (New York: Pantheon Books, 1983), pp. 78-104. Elias details how the king weaponized etiquette to monopolize the distribution of prestige, permanently domesticating the warrior nobility. The raw, kinetic violence of the warband had been entirely transmuted into psychological, courtly anxiety, fueled by the King's gaze and his distribution of tryphe (luxury and pensions).

div.head: 8.5.4 Kullaba Tension and the Pious E-Anna
div.p: The tension with the Catholic Kullaba was real, though highly manageable in the early decades of the reign. Leading clerics, such as the formidable Archbishop Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, frequently protested the overt immorality of the maîtresses-en-titre, particularly the reigning favorite, Madame de Montespan.Bossuet famously refused to grant absolution to Montespan, insisting on the primacy of the Catholic sacrament of marriage over the King's charismatic, extra-legal arrangements. See Jean Meyer, Bossuet (Paris: Plon, 1993), pp. 150-165. In the latter part of his reign, suffering military setbacks and personal aging, Louis signaled a definitive step in the direction of Catholic piety and Kullaba orthodoxy.

Yet, his E-Anna reflexes were by now so deeply ingrained that the medium through which this pious message was transmitted was yet another mistress: Madame de Maintenon. Even when submitting to the Church, the French BDMB could only bring himself to do so through the mediation of an extra-legal, charismatic female avatar, physically elevating her to unassailable power within the Great House.

div.head: 8.5.5 The End of the Line: The Fall of the BDMB in Europe
div.p: Louis XIV would prove to be the last truly successful BDMB in Europe to operate the dual sovereignty engine in its classical configuration. By the 18th century, the model was rapidly buckling under the relentless pressure of Reformed Christianity, the Enlightenment, and the rising merchant classes (the laboratores asserting political dominance). In England, this transition was managed relatively peacefully through the Glorious Revolution (1688), which permanently subordinated the charismatic monarch to the constitutional Kullaba of Parliament.

In France, because the E-Anna had been so thoroughly concentrated at Versailles, the system could not reform itself. The thermodynamic pressure eventually triggered a catastrophic explosion: the French Revolution (1789). By violently decapitating the BDMB and his queen, the revolutionaries attempted to establish a pure, rationalist Kullaba state. However, as the subsequent rise of Napoleon would instantly prove, eradicating the E-Anna by force without establishing a deeply internalized constitutional glove merely guarantees its immediate, terrifying resurrection.
